query: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but very poor room-temperature ductility, while its irradiation resistance has primarily been proposed by first-principles calculations. What intervention could improve its room-temperature ductility without compromising its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline under room-temperature, 1600 °C, and irradiation assessments, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Applying an intermediate-temperature thermomechanical treatment consisting of controlled rolling/forging followed by a short anneal at 800–1000 °C will refine the grain/subgrain structure in NbMoTaW, thereby enhancing dislocation mobility and increasing room‐temperature ductility without compromising its high‐temperature strength or irradiation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW produced via conventional casting with coarse grain structure.
generation.intervention: Intermediate-temperature rolling/forging followed by a short, moderate-temperature anneal (800–1000 °C for minutes).
generation.conditions: Evaluated under room-temperature tensile deformation, high-temperature mechanical testing at ~1600 °C, and controlled ion irradiation exposures.
generation.structural_mediator: Refined grain and subgrain structures with partial recrystallization that preserve the single-phase BCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced room-temperature ductility is achieved by increasing slip system activation through a refined microstructure which facilitates dislocation mobility, while the short anneal prevents the formation of deleterious secondary phases, thus maintaining high-temperature mechanical strength and irradiation resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Treated samples will exhibit increased plastic deformation at room temperature relative to the untreated state, retain comparable mechanical properties at 1600 °C, and show similar irradiation-induced defect behavior as the baseline alloy.
generation.baseline: Untreated, conventionally cast NbMoTaW with its original coarse-grained BCC structure exhibiting poor room-temperature ductility.
generation.boundary: The intervention must be optimized so that annealing times and temperatures remain short and moderate to avoid grain coarsening or secondary phase precipitation; the treatment is limited to processing conditions that do not induce phase transformations.
generation.uncertainty: The exact improvement in room-temperature ductility and the quantitative retention of high-temperature strength and irradiation tolerance require experimental validation, as precise thresholds are not yet established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of NbMoTaW samples: one untreated (baseline) and one processed by intermediate-temperature rolling/forging followed by a short anneal at 800–1000 °C. Subject both sets to standardized room-temperature tensile tests, high-temperature mechanical tests at ~1600 °C, and ion irradiation experiments. Analyze microstructural changes using TEM and EBSD to verify grain refinement without secondary phase formation.
measurements: High-temperature yield strength and ductility measurements at 1600 °C
Post-irradiation defect density and hardness measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in room-temperature ductility compared to the baseline, or if they exhibit decreased high-temperature strength or increased irradiation-induced defects relative to the untreated alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Developing lightweight alloys with excellent strength and ductility is always the objective for the application of structural alloys due to the demand for high-performance superalloys in increased harsh working conditions. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) and multiprincipal element alloys have received considerable interest for community experts and have become a worldwide hot spot since Cantor and Yeh reported their first publication [,]. Cr-containing HEAs have exhibited promising potential when applied in high-temperature industrial fields as a result of their remarkable strength [,,,], favorable ductility [,,], distinguished corrosion resistance [,,], superior wear and oxidation resistance [,,], and acceptable thermal stability [,]. Developing alloys with ultrahigh strength and excellent ductility simultaneously over a wide temperature range is crucial for developing high-temperature steam turbines [,,]. Recently, as a category of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), dual-phase high-entropy alloys (DP-HEAs) with a soft FCC phase and hard BCC (B2) phase have been reported to have excellent strength–ductility synergy at ambient temperature and high temperature [,,,,,,,,,], and thus have great potential to be used as steam turbine hot end components. Unfortunately, due to the rapid softening of the phase with the BCC structure at high temperatures, the yield strength of the alloy will significantly decrease [,,,,,]. Moreover, due to the weakness of grain boundaries and phase boundaries, the cracks initiate rapidly and propagate along the interface during high-temperature deformation, severely limiting the high-temperature application of FCC/B2 dual-phase high-entropy alloys [,,,,].

decision.trend: Early work (PMC4510962, 2015) showed that refining grain size and forming nanostructured columns in refractory HEA thin films or micropillars could enhance room-temperature ductility while preserving high-temperature stability. Subsequently (PMC5995863, 2018) demonstrated targeted B2 + BCC microstructural engineering to achieve improved RT ductility in otherwise brittle refractory high-entropy alloys. Later studies (PMC11206460, 2020) probed the temperature-dependent elastic and plastic behavior of single-phase BCC refractory HEAs, emphasizing edge-dislocation-dominated deformation at elevated temperatures. Most recently (PMC10894205, 2024) tied ductile vs. brittle behavior to intrinsic factors such as lattice distortion and dislocation core energies, specifically comparing VNbMoTaW with RHEAs containing hexagonal elements. Although these efforts highlight the value of microstructural refinements and tailored phase architectures for enhancing ductility, direct experiments coupling both high-temperature performance and irradiation tolerance remain incomplete.
decision.unsolved: Despite knowing that targeted microstructures can alleviate brittleness at ambient conditions and preserve high-temperature strength in refractory high-entropy alloys, a direct route to simultaneously ensure improved room-temperature ductility and validated irradiation resistance (beyond theoretical predictions) in single-phase BCC NbMoTaW remains unknown.
decision.lever: Perform intermediate-temperature rolling or forging followed by a short, moderate-temperature anneal (~800–1000 °C) to refine grain/subgrain structures. Control the annealing duration (on the order of minutes) to avoid forming stable secondary phases yet achieve partial recrystallization, enhancing slip activity at low temperatures while preserving high-temperature strength and minimal radiation-induced defect accumulation.
decision.why: Prior work (particularly PMC4510962 and PMC5995863) shows that refined or partially recrystallized refractory HEA microstructures can improve ductility without drastically sacrificing high-temperature properties. The short anneal avoids extensive grain growth or second-phase formation, thereby retaining the beneficial single-phase BCC structure implicated in robust irradiation resistance. A falsification experiment would involve subjecting both the baseline and treated samples to room-temperature tension, high-temperature compression at ~1600 °C, and ion-irradiation experiments followed by defect and hardness assessments. If the treated samples do not show improved RT ductility alongside comparable high-temperature strength and damage tolerance, the hypothesis would be disproven.
